en: The Sūtra on King Piliśāni’s Ten Dreams, translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time,...
King Piliyasanī slept at night and saw ten things in a dream.
What were these ten things?

First, he dreamed of three jars placed side by side; the two jars on either side were full and their vapors issued forth, flowing back and forth between them, yet they did not enter the empty jar in the center.
Second, he dreamed that a horse was eating from its mouth and also eating from its rump.
Third, he dreamed that a small tree blossomed with flowers.
Fourth, he dreamed that a small tree bore fruit.
Fifth, he dreamed of a man seeking a rope; behind the man was a sheep, which ate the rope as it was being offered.
Sixth, he dreamed of a fox sitting upon a golden bed, eating from a golden vessel.
Seventh, he dreamed that a great bull returned to drink milk from its own calf.

Eighth, he dreamed that four oxen came bellowing from the four directions, charging toward one another as if about to fight; yet, just before they were to meet, they vanished, and their whereabouts were unknown.
Ninth, he dreamed of a large pond whose center was turbid while its four edges were clear.
Tenth, he dreamed of a great mountain stream flowing a deep crimson.
Having seen these things, the king immediately awoke, struck with great terror that his kingdom, his person, his wife, and his children would be lost.
The next day, the king immediately summoned his high ministers, great officials, and various practitioners of the Way who were skilled at interpreting dreams, and asked them:
"Last night while sleeping, I had a dream of ten matters such as these. Upon waking, I was struck with terror and my mind was ill at ease. Who among you can interpret this dream?"
Among the various practitioners, there was a brahmin who said:
"I can explain this for the king, but I fear that if the king hears it, he will become sorrowful and unhappy.
The king said:
"Speak exactly as you have seen, without any concealment," the king said. The Brahmin replied, "The King's dreams are all evil and not auspicious.
You must take your most beloved queen, the crown prince, and those close to you—attendants and servants—and kill them all to offer as a sacrifice to the gods; only then can the King escape harm."
"The King possesses bedding and various precious, fine objects worn upon his person; all these should be burned as an offering to the gods. By doing so, the King’s person may be spared from harm.
When the King heard the Brahmin interpret the dream in this manner, he became deeply distressed and unhappy, withdrawing into his chamber of fasting to contemplate the matter.
The King had a chief queen named Maṇi, who went to the King’s presence and asked him:
"Why have you entered the fasting chamber so sorrowful and unhappy? Have I committed some offense against you?"
The king said, "You have done nothing wrong toward me; it is I myself who am grieving.
The lady asked again:
"For what reason is the King so sorrowful?
The King replied, "Do not question me; hearing this would cause you displeasure."
The lady spoke again:
"I am half of the King's body; if there were any good or evil [to befall him], the King ought to inform me—why then do you not speak to me?
The King then explained it to the lady:
"Last night I saw ten things in a dream; having awakened from the dream, I am filled with great sorrow and fear, for I dread the loss of my kingdom, as well as my own life, wife, and children."
I summoned my ministers, high officials, and various practitioners of the Way, and recounted to them the ten matters of my dream. A certain Brahmin interpreted the dream for me, saying:

"You must take your beloved and esteemed queen, the crown prince, and those close to you—attendants, servants, and slaves—as well as the white elephant and the famous horses, and kill them all to offer as sacrifice to the gods. Furthermore, burn your bedding, clothing, and precious jewels to offer as sacrifice to the gods; only then can the King’s person remain free from harm."
"It is for this reason that I am sorrowful and find no joy.
The lady said,
"O King, do not be sorrowful!"

It is like a person buying gold who grinds it on a whetstone; whether it is fine or coarse, good or bad, its color reveals itself upon the stone. Now the Buddha is nearby at the vihāra, not far from the capital; why do you not go there to ask about the meaning of your dream?
"You should follow what the Buddha understands.

The king immediately commanded his attendants and ministers to prepare the carriage and set out. Upon reaching the Buddha’s location, he proceeded on foot; the king alighted from his vehicle and approached the Buddha, prostrating himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet. He then withdrew to sit down and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Last night, I saw ten things in a dream."
First, he dreamed of three jars placed side by side; the two jars on either side were full, and their vapors flowed back and forth between them, yet did not enter the empty jar in the center.
Second, he dreamed of a horse eating from its mouth while its rump was also eating.
Third, he dreamed that small trees blossomed with flowers.
Fourth, he dreamed that small trees bore fruit.
Fifth, he dreamed of a man seeking a rope; behind the man was a sheep, which proceeded to eat the rope.
Sixth, he dreamed that a fox sat upon a golden couch and ate from a golden vessel.
Seventh, he dreamed that a great bull turned back to suckle at its own calf.
Eighth, he dreamed that four oxen came bellowing from the four directions, rushing toward one another as if to fight; yet as they drew near, they did not join, and their whereabouts became unknown.
"Ninth, I dreamed of a great pond whose center was turbid while its four edges were clear.
Tenth, I dreamed of a mountain stream flowing a deep crimson.

My dreams were thus; upon waking, I was struck with terror, fearing for my kingdom, my life, and my wife and children. May the Buddha explain these ten matters of my dream, and I pray to hear your instructions."
The Buddha said:
"Do not worry, O King!
Your dreams portend nothing other than this; what you have dreamed concerns matters of future generations, not of the present age."
The Buddha said:

"In future generations, people will not fear the prohibitions of the Dharma; they will be licentious, greedy for profit, and jealous, never knowing contentment. They will possess little righteousness or principle and lack a heart of compassion, being ignorant of shame or remorse regarding their joys and angers."
The Buddha said:

"First, as for the dream of seeing three jars placed together, with the two side jars full and their vapors flowing back and forth without entering the empty jar in the center—this refers to the wealthy and noble people of future generations who follow one another while disregarding the poor; it is precisely this that the King has seen in his dream."
"O King, do not fear, do not fear!
No harm shall come to the kingdom, nor to the crown prince,
nor to the queen," the Buddha said.

"Second, as for the King's dream of seeing a horse eating from its mouth and also eating from its rump: in future generations, those who become emperors, kings, and great ministers will receive grain and stipends from the government while simultaneously plundering the myriad people; they do not know contentment. That the King dreamed of a horse eating from its mouth and also eating from its rump refers precisely to this."
"O King, do not fear, do not fear!
No harm shall come to the kingdom, nor to the crown prince,
nor to the queen," the Buddha said.

"Third, as for the dream of seeing small trees blooming with flowers: it refers to people of future generations who, before their thirtieth year has passed, will have white hair growing on their heads; though young, they will be lustful and full of desire, aging prematurely. It is precisely this that the King saw in his dream of small trees blooming with flowers."
"O King, do not fear, do not fear!
No harm shall come to the kingdom, nor to the crown prince,
nor to the queen," the Buddha said.

"Fourth, as for the king’s dream of a small tree bearing fruit: in future generations, women will give birth to children and return home while still under fifteen years of age; they will not know shame or modesty. This is precisely what the king saw in his dream of the small tree bearing fruit."
"O King, do not fear!
No harm shall come to the kingdom, nor to the crown prince,
nor to the queen," the Buddha said.

"Fifth, as for the dream of seeing a person seeking a rope, with a sheep behind them that eats the rope: this refers to those people of later generations who, when their husbands go abroad on business, leave their wives behind, whereupon the wives engage in sexual relations with men of other households and consume their wealth. The person seen by the King in his dream seeking the rope is precisely this."
"O King, do not fear!
No harm shall come to you, to your kingdom, to your crown prince,
or to your queen," the Buddha said.

"Sixth, as for the king’s dream of seeing a fox sitting upon a golden couch and eating from a golden vessel: this signifies that in future generations, those of lowly status will become more honorable and possess wealth, such that the masses will revere them; whereas the descendants of dukes and marquises will become poorer and more humble, occupying lower seats and eating last. The king’s dream of the fox sitting on the golden couch and eating from the golden vessel refers precisely to this."
"O King, do not fear!
No harm shall come to you, nor to the crown prince, nor to the queen.
Thus spoke the Buddha.

"Seventh, as for the king’s dream that he saw a great ox suckling from its own calf: in future generations, people will lack propriety and righteousness; mothers will instead act as matchmakers for their daughters, luring men from other families to have sexual relations with them, selling their daughters for wealth and goods to provide for themselves, all without shame. The king’s dream of the great ox suckling from its calf refers precisely to this."
"O King, do not fear!
No harm shall come to the kingdom, nor to the crown prince,
nor to the queen," the Buddha said.

"Eighth, as for the dream of seeing four oxen coming from the four directions, bellowing and rushing toward one another as if about to fight, yet before they have met, the oxen vanish and their whereabouts are unknown: this signifies that in future generations, emperors, kings, high officials, and the common people will all lack a heart of utmost sincerity. Instead, they will practice further deception, fraud, folly, and malice, showing no reverence for Heaven and Earth. Because of this, the rains will not fall in their proper seasons. When high officials and the people offer prayers and supplications for rain, clouds shall rise from the four directions accompanied by thunder and the sound of lightning; the officials and the people will all say it is about to rain, but in an instant the clouds disperse and the rain departs without falling."
Why is this so? It is because the sovereign, the high officials, and the people lack loyalty, integrity, compassion, and benevolence.

As for the King’s dream of seeing four oxen bellowing and rushing toward one another, about to join but not yet joined, and being unable to find where the oxen are—this refers precisely to this situation.
"O King, do not fear!
No harm shall come to the kingdom, nor to the crown prince,
nor to the queen," the Buddha said.

"Ninth, as for the king’s dream of a large pond whose center was turbid while its four edges were clear: in future generations, the central lands shall be in turmoil and governance shall be unjust; the people will be unfilial toward their parents and disrespectful toward their elders. Meanwhile, the borderlands shall be peaceful and clear, and the people there will be harmonious and filial toward their two parents. This dream of the king’s, of the large pond with a turbid center and clear edges, refers precisely to this."
"O King, do not fear!
No harm shall come to the kingdom, nor to the crown prince,
nor to the queen," the Buddha said.

"Tenth, as for the king’s dream that a great mountain stream flowed with perfectly red water: in future generations, the various kingdoms shall fall into strife and contention; they shall raise armies and gather multitudes to attack and subdue one another. They shall engage in battle using chariots, infantry, and cavalry, killing and wounding one another in numbers beyond reckoning. The blood of the dead flowing along the roads will be perfectly red; this is precisely what the king saw in his dream of the great mountain stream flowing with perfectly red water."
"O King, do not fear!
No harm shall come to the kingdom, nor to the crown prince,
nor to the queen," the Buddha said.
"The things the King has seen in his dream are all matters pertaining to future lives, not matters of this present life; therefore, let the King not be afraid or grieve.
The King then knelt down and said, "Having received the Buddha’s teaching, my heart is filled with joy.

It is like a person holding a small vessel to contain oil; when the oil is abundant and the vessel too small, they seek a larger vessel to hold it, thereby becoming secure and no longer fearing. Now, having received the Buddha’s grace, I have attained peace."
The king immediately paid homage to the Buddha and returned to his palace, where he bestowed further rewards upon his principal consort and confiscated the stipends of all the high ministers.
The king declared:
"From this day forward, I shall no longer believe the words of various heterodox practitioners or Brahmins."
The Scripture on King Piliyakkhana’s Ten Dreams.
